questions.q: How is Immunity defined in the uploaded presentation?
options: A) The resistance of an organism to infection, disease, or other unwanted biological invasion.
B) The passive, temporary transfer of preformed monoclonal antibodies across the blood-brain barrier.
C) The non-specific breakdown of dietary proteins in the gastrointestinal tract.
D) The irreversible suppression of bone marrow stem cells following viral exposure.
questions.hint: Resistance of an organism to infection, disease, or unwanted biological invasion.
questions.explanation: Immunity is defined as the resistance of an organism to infection, disease, or other unwanted biological invasion.

questions.q: What are the primary functions of the immune system regarding self and non-self molecules?
options: A) It synthesizes non-essential amino acids and filters metabolic waste from renal tubules.
B) It distinguishes self from non-self, eliminates potentially harmful non-self molecules/cells, and recognizes and destroys abnormal cells derived from host tissues.
C) It promotes autoimmune destruction of vascular endothelium to regulate blood pressure.
D) It prevents all leukocyte migration during active bacterial infections.
questions.hint: Distinguish self from non-self, eliminate harmful non-self, and destroy abnormal host cells.
questions.explanation: The immune system distinguishes self from non-self, eliminates harmful non-self entities, and recognizes and destroys abnormal host-derived cells.

questions.q: According to the source, how is an Antigen (Ag) defined?
options: A) An enzyme produced by B-lymphocytes that neutralizes bacterial toxins.
B) A lipid hormone secreted by the adrenal cortex to suppress fever.
C) Any molecule capable of being recognized by the immune system.
D) A structural protein found exclusively on the inner nuclear membrane of erythrocytes.
questions.hint: Any molecule that can be recognized by the immune system.
questions.explanation: An antigen is defined as any molecule capable of being recognized by the immune system.

questions.q: Which components constitute the FIRST line of defense in non-specific (innate) immunity?
options: A) T-lymphocytes, B-lymphocytes, and memory cells.
B) Phagocytic leukocytes, fever, and the complement cascade.
C) Monoclonal immunoglobulins and plasma cells.
D) Skin, mucous membranes, and secretions of skin and mucous membranes.
questions.hint: Physical and chemical surface barriers: skin, mucous membranes, and their secretions.
questions.explanation: The first line of innate defense consists of anatomical and chemical barriers: skin, mucous membranes, and their secretions.

questions.q: Which components form the SECOND line of defense within non-specific (innate) mechanisms?
options: A) Phagocytic leukocytes, antimicrobial proteins, inflammatory response, and fever.
B) Skin, cerumen wax, and gastric hydrochloric acid.
C) Sensitized CD4+ and CD8+ T-lymphocytes.
D) Natural active contact with disease pathogens.
questions.hint: Phagocytic leukocytes, antimicrobial proteins, inflammation, and fever.
questions.explanation: The second line of innate defense comprises phagocytic leukocytes, antimicrobial proteins, the inflammatory reaction, and fever.

questions.q: What elements represent the THIRD line of defense (specific/adaptive immunity)?
options: A) Lysozymes, properdin, and stomach acid.
B) Lymphocytes, antibodies, and memory cells.
C) Epithelial surfaces of the respiratory and vaginal tracts.
D) Neutrophils, eosinophils, and basophils.
questions.hint: Adaptive immunity relies on lymphocytes, antibodies, and memory cells.
questions.explanation: Specific (adaptive) immunity constitutes the third line of defense and relies on lymphocytes, antibodies, and memory cells.

questions.q: What is an example of Natural Passive Acquired Immunity?
options: A) Active infection with a wild pathogen.
B) Administration of routine viral vaccines.
C) Maternal antibody transfer across the placenta or through mother's milk.
D) Infusion of hyperimmune serum.
questions.hint: Antibodies transferred naturally via the placenta or breast milk.
questions.explanation: Natural passive acquired immunity occurs naturally via transplacental IgG transfer or ingestion of IgA in colostrum/mother's milk.

questions.q: Which chemical secretions are listed as mechanisms of innate immunity?
options: A) Interleukin-2 and Interferon-gamma.
B) Monoclonal IgG and IgE antibodies.
C) Antinuclear antibodies and rheumatoid factor.
D) Oils and sweat, lysozymes, properdine, leukins, beta lysine, HCl, bile, and cerumen wax.
questions.hint: Look for oils/sweat, lysozymes, properdine, leukins, beta lysine, HCl, bile, and cerumen.
questions.explanation: Innate chemical barriers include cutaneous oils/sweat, lysozymes, properdine, leukins, beta lysine, gastric HCl, bile, and cerumen wax.

questions.q: How is an Antibody defined in the provided source?
options: A) A specific substance produced by the body in response to an antigen to defend the body.
B) A foreign structural polysaccharide that triggers tissue damage.
C) A hormone secreted by the thymus to stimulate granulopoiesis.
D) An intracellular receptor that blocks viral mRNA transcription.
questions.hint: A protective substance made by the body in response to an antigen.
questions.explanation: An antibody is a substance synthesized by the body in response to a specific antigen to defend the host.

questions.q: Into what four major clinical categories are immune system disorders classified?
options: A) Anemia, Leukopenia, Thrombocytopenia, and Pancytopenia.
B) Immunodeficiency, Gammapathy, Hypersensitivity, and Autoimmunity.
C) Rhinitis, Asthma, Urticaria, and Anaphylaxis.
D) Primary, Secondary, Tertiary, and Quaternary dysfunctions.
questions.hint: Immunodeficiency, gammapathy, hypersensitivity, and autoimmunity.
questions.explanation: Immune system dysfunctions are categorized into four major types: Immunodeficiency, Gammapathy, Hypersensitivity, and Autoimmunity.

questions.q: What characterizes the PRIMARY Immune Response when the body encounters an invader for the FIRST time?
options: A) Immediate, maximal antibody production within 30 seconds.
B) Instantaneous destruction of all antigens by memory T-cells.
C) No measurable immune response for the first few days, followed by steady antibody growth over the next 10–15 days.
D) Complete absence of lymphocyte involvement.
questions.hint: A lag of a few days with no measurable response, then steady rise over 10–15 days.
questions.explanation: During a primary immune response, there is a lag period with no measurable response for the first few days, followed by steady antibody synthesis over 10–15 days.

questions.q: What distinguishes the SECONDARY Immune Response from the primary response upon re-exposure to an antigen?
options: A) It is significantly slower and generates fewer antibodies.
B) It relies exclusively on innate epithelial barriers.
C) It causes immediate atrophy of secondary lymphoid organs.
D) It is a more rapid response where antibody production increases dramatically in a much shorter time period.
questions.hint: Faster onset and a dramatic surge in antibodies over a shorter period.
questions.explanation: The secondary immune response is rapid and produces dramatically higher antibody titers over a shorter duration due to immunological memory.

questions.q: What defines Immunodeficiency?
options: A) A state in which the ability of the immune system to fight infectious disease and cancer is compromised or entirely absent.
B) An overactive immune response directed exclusively against ingested food proteins.
C) The physiological elevation of blood white blood cells during exercise.
D) A benign, temporary accumulation of plasma cells in the spleen.
questions.hint: Compromised or absent ability of the immune system to fight infection and cancer.
questions.explanation: Immunodeficiency is a state where immune capacity to combat pathogens and malignant neoplasms is impaired or absent.

questions.q: What is the fundamental origin of PRIMARY Immunodeficiency disorders?
options: A) Environmental toxin exposure in geriatric populations.
B) Intrinsic, inherited defects in the immune system (often gene mutations), usually manifesting in infants and young children.
C) High-dose antineoplastic chemotherapy for solid tumors.
D) Chronic end-stage renal disease.
questions.hint: Intrinsic, inherited gene defects usually seen in infants and young children.
questions.explanation: Primary immunodeficiencies stem from intrinsic, inherited gene defects/mutations and typically present during infancy or early childhood.

questions.q: Which conditions are listed as specific genetic examples of PRIMARY Immunodeficiency?
options: A) AIDS, Multiple Myeloma, and Leukemia.
B) Diabetes mellitus, Severe burns, and Malnutrition.
C) X-linked agammaglobulinemia (XLA), Common variable immunodeficiency (CVID), and Severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID).
D) Goodpasture syndrome, Graves disease, and Myasthenia gravis.
questions.hint: XLA, CVID, and SCID.
questions.explanation: X-linked agammaglobulinemia, CVID, and SCID are classic primary immunodeficiencies caused by intrinsic genetic mutations.

questions.q: What causes SECONDARY Immunodeficiency disorders?
options: A) Congenital chromosomal deletions present at conception.
B) Overproduction of polyclonal IgM immunoglobulins.
C) Inborn errors of amino acid metabolism.
D) Outside sources or underlying chronic illnesses that interfere with the normal growth or expression of the immune system later in life.
questions.hint: External factors or chronic illnesses acquired later in life.
questions.explanation: Secondary immunodeficiencies develop later in life secondary to external factors (chemotherapy, radiation, toxins) or chronic systemic diseases.

questions.q: Which underlying causes and diseases are categorized as SECONDARY Immunodeficiencies?
options: A) Severe burns, chemotherapy, radiation, diabetes, malnutrition, AIDS, leukemia, and multiple myeloma.
B) XLA, CVID, and SCID.
C) Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis and serum sickness.
D) Atopy, allergic rhinitis, and asthma.
questions.hint: Burns, chemotherapy, radiation, diabetes, malnutrition, AIDS, leukemia, and multiple myeloma.
questions.explanation: Extrinsic insults like burns, chemotherapy, radiation, malnutrition, HIV/AIDS, and hematological malignancies cause secondary immunodeficiency.

questions.q: What key feature distinguishes Monoclonal Gammapathy from Polyclonal Gammapathy?
options: A) Monoclonal involves T-cell apoptosis; Polyclonal involves neutrophil lysis.
B) Monoclonal involves overproduction of ONE class of immunoglobulins; Polyclonal involves overproduction of VIRTUALLY ALL classes of immunoglobulins.
C) Monoclonal occurs only in neonates; Polyclonal occurs only in the elderly.
D) Monoclonal is caused by fungal infection; Polyclonal is caused by helminths.
questions.hint: Monoclonal = one class of immunoglobulins; Polyclonal = virtually all classes.
questions.explanation: Monoclonal gammapathy is the single-clone overproduction of one immunoglobulin class, whereas polyclonal gammapathy exhibits elevation across virtually all classes.

questions.q: How is Hypersensitivity defined in the text?
options: A) Complete absence of antibody production following antigen exposure.
B) Normal physiological inflammation restricted to wound healing.
C) An exaggerated and/or pathological immune response to exogenous or endogenous substances.
D) Passive neutralization of bacterial toxins by complement proteins.
questions.hint: An exaggerated or pathological immune response to foreign or self substances.
questions.explanation: Hypersensitivity is defined as an exaggerated or pathological immune response to foreign or self substances.

questions.q: What is the definition of Allergy provided in the source?
options: A) An autoimmune reaction against nuclear DNA-protein complexes.
B) A congenital absence of phagocytic leukocytes.
C) A bacterial bloodstream invasion leading to septic shock.
D) An abnormal immunological response to an otherwise harmless environmental stimulus (e.g., food, pollen, animal dander).
questions.hint: An abnormal immune response to an otherwise harmless environmental antigen.
questions.explanation: Allergy is specifically defined as an abnormal immune response to an otherwise harmless environmental antigen.

questions.q: Which clinical manifestations are characteristic signs of Immunodeficiency in pediatric patients?
options: A) Opportunistic infections, recurrent pneumonia, bronchitis, sinus/ear infections, growth/developmental delay, oral ulcers, and digestive problems.
B) Isolated hypertension, obesity, and hyperkeratosis.
C) Polycythemia, splenomegaly, and bounding pulses.
D) Rapid hair growth and joint hypermobility.
questions.hint: Recurrent or opportunistic infections, growth/developmental delay, oral ulcers, and GI problems.
questions.explanation: Immunodeficiency presents with recurrent or opportunistic sinopulmonary infections, delayed growth, blood disorders, and mucocutaneous lesions.

questions.q: What therapeutic modalities are listed for managing and boosting the immune system in Immunodeficiency disorders?
options: A) High-dose antimetabolites and radiation therapy.
B) Immunoglobulin therapy, Interferon-gamma therapy, Growth factors, and Stem cell transplantation.
C) Long-term oral antihistamines and decongestants exclusively.
D) Surgical splenectomy and phlebotomy.
questions.hint: Immunoglobulin therapy, interferon-gamma, growth factors, and stem cell transplantation.
questions.explanation: Immunodeficiency management includes infection control, immunoglobulin replacement, interferon-gamma, hematopoietic growth factors, and stem cell transplantation.

questions.q: In the context of hypersensitivity, what defines the 'Sensitization' phase?
options: A) Severe anaphylactic shock occurring upon initial antigen contact.
B) The rapid degranulation of basophils without prior antibody production.
C) The initial, asymptomatic contact with an antigen that produces an immune response.
D) Delayed tissue necrosis mediated by cytotoxic T-cells 10 years after exposure.
questions.hint: The initial, asymptomatic contact with an antigen that primes an immune response.
questions.explanation: Sensitization is the initial, clinically silent exposure to an antigen that induces antibody formation or T-cell priming.

questions.q: What is the cellular mechanism and antibody type driving TYPE I (Immediate) Hypersensitivity?
options: A) IgM binding to cell surface antigens leading to complement lysis.
B) Circulating IgG-antigen immune complexes depositing in blood vessels.
C) Presensitized CD4+ T-cells releasing inflammatory cytokines.
D) Preformed IgE antibodies coating mast cells and basophils that are crosslinked by free antigen, causing cell degranulation and histamine release.
questions.hint: Antigen crosslinks IgE on mast cells/basophils, triggering histamine release.
questions.explanation: Type I hypersensitivity is mediated by antigen crosslinking of IgE on mast cells/basophils, triggering immediate degranulation of histamine and mediators.

questions.q: Which clinical conditions are classic examples of TYPE I (Immediate) Hypersensitivity?
options: A) Asthma, Allergic rhinitis, Atopy, Anaphylaxis, Food allergies, and Insect venom allergies.
B) Autoimmune hemolytic anemia, ITP, and Goodpasture syndrome.
C) Serum sickness, Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, and SLE.
D) Contact dermatitis, Mantoux tuberculin test, and Type 1 Diabetes.
questions.hint: Asthma, allergic rhinitis, atopy, anaphylaxis, food allergies, and insect stings.
questions.explanation: Type I reactions include allergic asthma, allergic rhinitis, systemic anaphylaxis, food allergies, and insect sting reactions.

questions.q: What immunologic mechanism defines TYPE II (Cytotoxic / Antibody-Mediated) Hypersensitivity?
options: A) IgE-mediated histamine release from basophils.
B) IgM or IgG antibodies binding to cell surface/tissue antigens, causing complement activation, phagocytosis, ADCC, or cellular dysfunction.
C) Deposition of circulating soluble immune complexes in small capillaries.
D) Direct CD8+ T-cell killing of uninfected somatic cells.
questions.hint: IgM or IgG binding to cell/tissue antigens.
questions.explanation: Type II hypersensitivity involves IgG/IgM binding to tissue/cell surface antigens, activating complement or cell-mediated destruction.

questions.q: Which diseases represent TYPE II Hypersensitivity involving DIRECT CELL DESTRUCTION?
options: A) Asthma and allergic rhinitis.
B) Serum sickness and hypersensitivity pneumonitis.
C) Acute hemolytic transfusion reaction, Autoimmune hemolytic anemia (AIHA), Hemolytic disease of the newborn, ITP, and Pernicious anemia.
D) Contact dermatitis and Stevens-Johnson syndrome.
questions.hint: Hemolytic transfusion reactions, AIHA, hemolytic disease of the newborn, ITP, and pernicious anemia.
questions.explanation: Cytotoxic Type II cell-destructive examples include hemolytic transfusion reactions, AIHA, fetal/neonatal hemolytic disease, ITP, and pernicious anemia.

questions.q: Which conditions are examples of TYPE II Hypersensitivity leading to INFLAMMATION or IMPAIRED CELLULAR FUNCTION?
options: A) Anaphylaxis and latex allergy.
B) Polyarteritis nodosa and IgA nephropathy.
C) Mantoux tuberculin test and Graft-versus-host disease.
D) Goodpasture syndrome, Rheumatic fever, Graves disease, Bullous pemphigoid, Pemphigus vulgaris, and Myasthenia gravis.
questions.hint: Goodpasture syndrome, rheumatic fever, Graves disease, pemphigoid/pemphigus, and myasthenia gravis.
questions.explanation: Type II inflammatory (Goodpasture, Rheumatic fever) and functional impairment disorders (Graves, Myasthenia gravis, Pemphigus) target tissue receptors/antigens.

questions.q: What sequence of events drives TYPE III (Immune Complex) Hypersensitivity?
options: A) IgG antibodies bind circulating antigens to form immune complexes that deposit in tissues, activate complement, attract neutrophils, and cause tissue lysis.
B) IgE crosslinks on mast cells causing localized edema.
C) CD4+ T-cells release IL-2 to stimulate epidermal hyperkeratosis.
D) Direct autoantibody destruction of thyroid follicular cells.
questions.hint: Circulating IgG-antigen immune complexes deposit in tissues, activate complement, and recruit neutrophils.
questions.explanation: Type III reactions occur when soluble circulating antigen-IgG complexes deposit in microvasculature, activating complement and recruiting destructive neutrophils.

questions.q: Which clinical entities are categorized as TYPE III (Immune Complex) Hypersensitivity?
options: A) Food allergy and anaphylaxis.

B) Serum sickness, Drug-induced vasculitis, Hypersensitivity pneumonitis, Polyarteritis Nodosa (PAN), Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN), IgA nephropathy, and Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE).
C) Pernicious anemia and Myasthenia gravis.
D) Nickel contact dermatitis and Multiple Sclerosis.
questions.hint: Serum sickness, vasculitis, hypersensitivity pneumonitis, PAN, PSGN, IgA nephropathy, and SLE.
questions.explanation: Type III immune complex-mediated diseases include serum sickness, vasculitis, PSGN, IgA nephropathy, PAN, and SLE.

questions.q: What pathophysiological mechanism defines TYPE IV (Delayed / T-Cell Mediated) Hypersensitivity?
options: A) Preformed IgE antibodies triggering immediate histamine release.
B) Complement activation by cell-bound IgM antibodies.
C) Contact of antigen with presensitized T-lymphocytes (CD4+ cells releasing cytokines to activate macrophages, or CD8+ cells causing direct cell cytotoxicity).
D) Accumulation of circulating antibody-antigen aggregates in glomeruli.
questions.hint: Presensitized T-cells (CD4+ activating macrophages or CD8+ direct cytotoxicity).
questions.explanation: Type IV hypersensitivity is cell-mediated: presensitized CD4+ T-cells activate macrophages via cytokines, while CD8+ T-cells exert direct cytotoxicity.

questions.q: Which clinical conditions and diagnostic tests represent TYPE IV (Delayed) Hypersensitivity?
options: A) Atopy and allergic transfusion reactions.
B) Autoimmune hemolytic anemia and Rheumatic fever.
C) Polyarteritis nodosa and Membranous nephropathy.

D) Acute/chronic transplant rejection, Contact dermatitis (nickel, poison ivy), Mantoux tuberculin skin test, SJS/TEN, DRESS, Multiple Sclerosis, Hashimoto's Thyroiditis, Rheumatoid Arthritis, and Type 1 Diabetes.
questions.hint: Transplant rejection, contact dermatitis, Mantoux test, SJS/TEN, DRESS, MS, Hashimoto's, RA, and Type 1 DM.
questions.explanation: Type IV cell-mediated reactions include contact dermatitis, tuberculin skin testing, transplant rejection, SJS/TEN, DRESS, and cell-mediated autoimmune diseases (MS, Type 1 DM, RA).

questions.q: Which respiratory signs and symptoms are listed as clinical manifestations of severe Hypersensitivity?
options: A) Rhinorrhea, sneezing, sinusitis, bronchospasm, dyspnea, tachypnea, wheezing, cyanosis, nasal flaring, and use of accessory muscles.
B) Isolated stridor with normal lung sounds.
C) Bradypnea and central apnea.
D) Productive cough with rusty sputum.
questions.hint: Rhinorrhea, sneezing, sinusitis, bronchospasm, dyspnea, tachypnea, wheezing, cyanosis, flaring, accessory muscles.
questions.explanation: Respiratory signs of hypersensitivity encompass upper mucosal symptoms (rhinorrhea, sneezing) and lower airway obstruction (bronchospasm, wheezing, accessory muscle use, cyanosis).

questions.q: What tegumentary (skin) clinical manifestations occur during Hypersensitivity reactions?
options: A) Hyperpigmentation and hyperkeratosis.
B) Edema, rashes, urticaria, angioedema, itching, diaphoresis, cyanosis, and skin discoloration.
C) Telangiectasias and jaundice.
D) Alopecia totalis and petechiae.
questions.hint: Edema, rashes, urticaria, angioedema, itching, diaphoresis, cyanosis, and discoloration.
questions.explanation: Cutaneous hypersensitivity features urticaria, angioedema, generalized pruritus, rash, and localized swelling.

questions.q: What specialized diagnostic tests are used specifically to identify environmental or food ALLERGENS in hypersensitivity evaluations?
options: A) Antinuclear antibody (ANA) and Lumbar puncture.
B) Bone marrow biopsy and Renal ultrasound.
C) Skin prick test, Intradermal test, Patch testing, Provocation testing, Eosinophil count, and Oral food challenges.
D) Direct Coombs test and Blood cultures.
questions.hint: Skin prick, intradermal, patch, provocation, eosinophil count, and oral food challenges.
questions.explanation: Allergen testing utilizes skin prick tests, intradermal/patch testing, provocation tests, eosinophil counts, and oral challenges.

questions.q: Which diagnostic blood tests are ordered in the laboratory evaluation of Hypersensitivity?
options: A) Blood urea nitrogen and Creatinine clearance.
B) Thyroid stimulating hormone and Thyroxine.
C) Cerebrospinal fluid protein and Glucose.
D) Complete blood count, Allergen-specific IgE blood tests, Histamine and Tryptase tests, Cytotoxic tests, and Genetic testing.
questions.hint: CBC, allergen-specific IgE, histamine and tryptase, cytotoxic tests, and genetic testing.
questions.explanation: Lab evaluation of hypersensitivity includes CBC (for eosinophilia), allergen-specific IgE, serum tryptase/histamine levels, and cytotoxic assays.

questions.q: What pharmacological classes and specific agents are listed for the GENERAL MANAGEMENT of Hypersensitivity reactions?
options: A) Antihistamines (Benadryl), Decongestants (Phenylephrine), Mast cell stabilizers (Cromolyn Sodium), Corticosteroids (Prednisolone, Dexamethasone), Adrenaline/Epinephrine, and Aminophylline/Theophylline.
B) Penicillin, Gentamicin, and Vancomycin.
C) Methotrexate, Cyclophosphamide, and Cisplatin.
D) Insulin, Glucagon, and Metformin.
questions.hint: Benadryl, phenylephrine, cromolyn sodium, prednisolone/dexamethasone, adrenaline/epinephrine, aminophylline/theophylline.
questions.explanation: Hypersensitivity management relies on H1-blockers, decongestants, mast cell stabilizers, corticosteroids, epinephrine, and bronchodilators.

questions.q: How is an Autoimmune Disorder defined in the provided source?
options: A) A primary genetic inability to produce functioning T-cell receptors.
B) A group of disorders in which tissue injury is caused by a humoral or cell-mediated immune response to self tissues (self antigens).
C) An acute bacterial infection of the lymphatic vessels.
D) A transient allergic response triggered by cold weather exposure.
questions.hint: Tissue injury caused by a humoral or cell-mediated immune response to self antigens.
questions.explanation: Autoimmune disorders occur when humoral or cellular immune effector mechanisms target and damage healthy self-tissues.

questions.q: What proposed etiology is discussed regarding the trigger for Autoimmune Disorders?
options: A) Ingestion of excessively pasteurized dairy products.
B) High exposure to ultraviolet radiation in neonates.
C) Microorganisms (bacteria or viruses) or drugs triggering changes that confuse the immune system in genetically susceptible individuals.
D) Complete absence of memory B-lymphocytes.
questions.hint: Microorganisms (bacteria/viruses) or drugs in genetically susceptible people.
questions.explanation: Autoimmunity is thought to be triggered by infectious pathogens or medications that alter self-antigens or induce molecular mimicry in genetically predisposed hosts.

questions.q: What three primary pathological consequences can result from an Autoimmune Disorder?
options: A) Intravascular hemolysis, systemic hypertension, and renal calculus formation.
B) Hyperthermia, muscle hypertrophy, and bone hyperostosis.
C) Hyperinsulinemia, hypocalcemia, and polycythemia.
D) Destruction of body tissue, abnormal growth of an organ, and changes in organ function.
questions.hint: Destruction of body tissue, abnormal organ growth, and changes in organ function.
questions.explanation: Autoimmune responses manifest pathologically via tissue destruction, dysregulated organ growth, or functional organ alterations.

questions.q: Which conditions are listed among the COMMON Autoimmune Disorders in the text?
options: A) Addison disease, Celiac disease, Dermatomyositis, Graves disease, Hashimoto Thyroiditis, IBD, Multiple sclerosis, Myasthenia gravis, Pernicious anemia, Reactive arthritis, Rheumatoid arthritis, Sjögren syndrome, SLE, and Type 1 Diabetes.
B) XLA, CVID, SCID, and Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome.
C) Asthma, Atopy, Urticaria, and Anaphylaxis.
D) Multiple Myeloma, Hodgkin Lymphoma, and Leukemia.
questions.hint: Addison, celiac, dermatomyositis, Graves, Hashimoto's, IBD, MS, myasthenia gravis, pernicious anemia, RA, Sjögren's, SLE, Type 1 DM.
questions.explanation: The source lists a comprehensive panel of systemic and organ-specific autoimmune disorders including Lupus, RA, MS, Celiac, Graves, and Type 1 DM.

questions.q: How are Autoimmune Diseases sub-classified based on the location of the autoimmune attack?
options: A) Acute vs Chronic.
B) Systemic (affecting many organs) vs Organ-Specific (affecting one main organ).
C) Congenital vs Neonatal.
D) Benign vs Malignant.
questions.hint: Systemic vs. organ-specific.
questions.explanation: Autoimmune diseases are anatomically classified as Systemic (multi-organ) or Organ-Specific (targeting a single organ/tissue).

questions.q: What defines SYSTEMIC Autoimmune Diseases, and what are typical examples?
options: A) Disorders where autoantigens are restricted to skin keratinocytes alone.
B) Disorders caused by acute bacterial toxin production in the gut.

C) Disorders where autoantigens (e.g., DNA-protein complexes) are found in almost any cell type, causing pathological damage across many organs; examples include Rheumatoid Arthritis, SLE, Scleroderma, and Dermatomyositis.
D) Conditions that resolve spontaneously within 48 hours without therapy.
questions.hint: Widespread autoantigens (like DNA-protein complexes) affecting many organs; e.g., RA, SLE, scleroderma, dermatomyositis.
questions.explanation: Systemic autoimmune diseases target ubiquitously expressed autoantigens (like nuclear complexes), resulting in widespread multi-organ injury (e.g., SLE, RA, Scleroderma).

questions.q: What defines ORGAN-SPECIFIC Autoimmune Diseases, and what specific organ-target pairs are listed?
options: A) Disorders involving generalized vasculitis of all large arteries.
B) Disorders where autoantibodies deposit exclusively in cardiac valves.
C) Disorders affecting only the central nervous system reticular activating system.

D) Disorders where a particular organ or tissue is preferentially targeted; examples include the Thyroid gland in Graves disease, Beta cells of the endocrine pancreas in Type 1 Diabetes, and Skin in Vitiligo.
questions.hint: Targets a specific organ/tissue, such as thyroid in Graves, pancreatic beta cells in Type 1 DM, or skin in vitiligo.
questions.explanation: Organ-specific autoimmunity focuses immune destruction on a single tissue/organ, such as thyroid tissue in Graves, pancreatic beta cells in Type 1 DM, or melanocytes in Vitiligo.

questions.q: Which general clinical manifestations are common across Autoimmune Diseases?
options: A) Fatigue, low-grade fever, hair loss, skin rashes, achy muscles, trouble concentrating, tissue overgrowth (psoriasis), swelling/redness, numbness/tingling in hands/feet, and general weakness.
B) High-grade fever with purpuric rash and neck stiffness exclusively.
C) Bounding peripheral pulses and severe hypertension.
D) Rapid weight gain and massive muscle hypertrophy.
questions.hint: Fatigue, low fever, hair loss, rashes, achy muscles, trouble concentrating, psoriasis, swelling/redness, numbness/tingling, weakness.
questions.explanation: Constitutional and neuromuscular features of autoimmunity include fatigue, low fever, myalgias, arthralgias, rashes, alopecia, and peripheral neuropathic symptoms.

questions.q: Which key LABORATORY tests are ordered during the diagnostic evaluation of suspected Autoimmune Diseases?
options: A) Serum IgE, Histamine levels, and Skin prick test.
B) Antinuclear antibody (ANA) tests, Autoantibody tests, FBP with WBC differential, Metabolic panel, CRP, ESR, and Urinalysis.
C) Blood cultures, Stool culture, and Viral PCR.
D) Sweat chloride test and Fractional excretion of sodium.
questions.hint: ANA, autoantibody tests, FBP with WBC differential, metabolic panel, CRP, ESR, and urinalysis.
questions.explanation: Autoimmune diagnostic panels rely on ANA screening, specific autoantibody titers, inflammatory markers (ESR, CRP), complete blood counts, metabolic profiles, and urinalysis.

questions.q: A 7-year-old boy presents with recurrent bacterial sinopulmonary infections, chronic diarrhea, and poor weight gain, with low serum IgG, IgA, and IgM and a mutation affecting B-cell development. Classify this immunodeficiency, state whether it is intrinsic or extrinsic, and name the primary treatment.
options: A) Secondary Immunodeficiency; Extrinsic; Give systemic chemotherapy.
B) Monoclonal Gammapathy; Intrinsic; Perform immediate splenectomy.
C) Primary Immunodeficiency; Intrinsic (inherited gene defect); Manage with Immunoglobulin Therapy (and infection control).
D) Type I Hypersensitivity; Extrinsic; Administer oral cromolyn sodium.
questions.hint: Genetic B-cell defect with low immunoglobulins = Primary (intrinsic) immunodeficiency; treat with immunoglobulin therapy.
questions.explanation: Recurrent infections with pan-hypogammaglobulinemia due to a genetic mutation represent a Primary (intrinsic) Immunodeficiency, treated with Immunoglobulin replacement therapy.

questions.q: A 10-year-old girl develops generalized hives, facial angioedema, wheezing, and hypotension 15 minutes after eating peanuts. Identify the hypersensitivity type, the key antibody/cell involved, and the emergency drug of choice.
options: A) Type II Cytotoxic Hypersensitivity; IgG and Neutrophils; Intravenous Penicillin.
B) Type III Immune Complex Hypersensitivity; Circulating IgM; Oral Prednisolone.
C) Type IV Delayed Hypersensitivity; Sensitized T-cells; Topical Cromolyn.
D) Type I Immediate Hypersensitivity; Preformed IgE on Mast cells/Basophils; Intramuscular Adrenaline / Epinephrine.
questions.hint: Rapid anaphylaxis after food = Type I immediate hypersensitivity (IgE + mast cells/basophils); give adrenaline/epinephrine.
questions.explanation: Rapid onset IgE-mediated anaphylaxis to food is a Type I Immediate reaction, requiring immediate Adrenaline/Epinephrine.

questions.q: A 12-year-old girl presents with persistent fatigue, low-grade fever, malar skin rash, arthralgias, proteinuria, positive ANA, and elevated ESR. Classify this condition, state whether it is systemic or organ-specific, and name the specific disease.
options: A) Autoimmune Disorder; Systemic; Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE).
B) Primary Immunodeficiency; Organ-specific; SCID.
C) Polyclonal Gammapathy; Systemic; Multiple Myeloma.
D) Type II Hypersensitivity; Organ-specific; Graves disease.
questions.hint: Multi-organ features with positive ANA = Systemic autoimmune disorder, Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE).
questions.explanation: Multi-organ involvement with nuclear autoantigens (ANA positive) defines Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE), a classic systemic autoimmune disease.

questions.q: A patient develops acute intravascular hemolysis within 30 minutes of an ABO-incompatible blood transfusion. What type of hypersensitivity is this, what mechanism destroys RBCs, and what condition shares this mechanism?
options: A) Type I Hypersensitivity; IgE degranulation; Allergic rhinitis.
B) Type III Hypersensitivity; Immune complex deposition in joints; Rheumatoid arthritis.
C) Type II (Cytotoxic) Hypersensitivity; IgM/IgG binding to RBC surface antigens activating complement lysis; Autoimmune Hemolytic Anemia (AIHA) or Hemolytic Disease of the Newborn.
D) Type IV Hypersensitivity; Sensitized CD8+ T-cell destruction; Contact dermatitis.
questions.hint: Antibody-mediated RBC destruction = Type II cytotoxic hypersensitivity; shared with AIHA and hemolytic disease of the newborn.
questions.explanation: Acute ABO transfusion mismatch is a Type II cytotoxic reaction (antibody binding + complement lysis), sharing mechanisms with AIHA and Hemolytic Disease of the Newborn.
